name: Bob Hope
tagline: English-born comedian who became America's entertainer-in-chief to its troops for fifty years

immigration.detail: Hope's father, a stonemason, moved the family of seven boys to Cleveland in 1908 in search of work. Leslie, then four, grew up selling newspapers and winning amateur talent contests; he became a U.S. citizen in 1920 through his father's naturalization.

summary: A stonemason's son from south London who grew up in Cleveland, Bob Hope conquered vaudeville, Broadway, radio, film and television, and spent every Christmas from 1941 to 1991 performing for American service members around the world, a devotion that led Congress to name him the first honorary veteran of the U.S. Armed Forces.

biography.text: Leslie Townes Hope was born in Eltham, in south-east London, on May 29, 1903, the fifth of seven sons of a stonemason and a Welsh light-opera singer. In 1908 the family emigrated to Cleveland, Ohio, where the boy sold newspapers, boxed briefly under the name Packy East, and won a Charlie Chaplin impersonation contest. He became an American citizen in 1920 when his father was naturalized.

Renamed Bob, he worked his way up through vaudeville in the 1920s, reached Broadway in Roberta (1933) and Ziegfeld Follies of 1936, and introduced the Cole Porter song 'It's De-Lovely'. In The Big Broadcast of 1938 he sang 'Thanks for the Memory', which became his lifelong theme. His NBC radio show, launched in 1938, made him one of the most listened-to voices in America.

Beginning with Road to Singapore (1940), Hope and Bing Crosby made seven 'Road' pictures that remain comedy classics, and Hope went on to appear in more than 50 films. He hosted the Academy Awards ceremony a record 19 times, joking that at his house Oscar night was known as 'Passover'.

In May 1941 Hope performed his first show for troops at March Field, California, and for the next fifty years he took his Christmas shows to service members in the Second World War, Korea, Vietnam, Lebanon and the Persian Gulf, logging millions of miles with the USO. 'For the first time in my life,' he wrote of his wartime tours, 'I was in a situation where they were giving me more than I was giving them.'

Congress awarded him a Congressional Gold Medal (presented by President Kennedy in 1963), President Johnson gave him the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1969, and in 1997 a joint resolution of Congress made him the first and only person named an honorary veteran of the U.S. Armed Forces. The Library of Congress holds his archive of more than 85,000 pages of jokes. He died at his home in Toluca Lake, California, on July 27, 2003, two months after his 100th birthday.

quotes.context: Title of Public Law 105-67, enacted October 30, 1997, the only such honour ever conferred

fun_facts.text: The Library of Congress preserves Hope's joke file: about 85,000 pages, organised by topic, which he kept in a fireproof vault.
Hope's first USO-style broadcast in 1941 was a radio show from an air base; the laughter was so loud that he made the troops his audience for the rest of the war.

discussion_prompts: Hope said the troops gave him more than he gave them. Why might making people laugh matter most in the hardest places?
He arrived as a four-year-old immigrant and became a symbol of America to soldiers abroad. What makes someone 'American' in other people's eyes?
Watch a clip from a 1950 television special. How has comedy changed since then, and what still works?

review_notes.ihh_statement: Bob Hope immigrated to Cleveland, Ohio, in 1920.
review_notes.finding: The family emigrated in 1908 (as the IHH infobox states); 1920 is the year he became a citizen. The biography text and infobox on the current page disagree.
